title: Beyond Borders
full_review:
An American living a sheltered life in London has her eyes opened to the suffering of the wider world when she becomes involved with a doctor passionately committed to relief efforts in war-torn countries in "Beyond Borders" (Paramount).

Despite the sincerity of its humanitarian message, director Martin Campbell's film suffers from severe narrative malnutrition, with characters less fleshed out than the famine victims they champion.

The public-awareness-sermon-wrapped-in-a-romance plot centers on Sarah Jordan (Angelina Jolie), an art dealer whose comfortable existence with Brit socialite hubby Henry Bauford (Linus Roache) is suddenly turned topsy-turvy at a 1984 black-tie fund-raiser honoring Henry's philanthropist father.

Removing the proverbial blinders from the lush-lipped Yank's eyes is Dr. Nick Callahan (Clive Owen), a firebrand with a stethoscope who marches unannounced into the posh bash and proceeds to take the elder Bauford to task for kowtowing to political pressure and putting the breaks on vital funding for his relief camp in Ethiopia. To punctuate his tongue-lashing, Callahan brings along an emaciated African lad whose life he saved, causing the well-heeled assembly to choke on their collective silver spoons.

Sarah finds herself bitten by the humanitarian bug. In rapid succession, she quits her job at a snobby gallery, empties her savings account in order to purchase food and medical supplies and charters a jet to Ethiopia. But nothing can prepare her for the swell of human misery she encounters at Callahan's triage camp, a sea of suffering which immediately lances her naivete with a dose of cold -- or in Saharan Africa, blisteringly hot -- reality.

Callahan is at first standoffish, convinced that the pampered American's altruistic epiphany is merely the knee-jerk response to a guilty conscience. But quicker than you can say "cholera," the two are in I'd-cross-an-Afghan-minefield-for-you love.

The remainder of the film -- which leapfrogs from 1984 to 1989 and then to 1995 -- seesaws between Sarah's failing marriage in London and her Third World humanitarian exploits, which she justifies as part of her new U.N. job, though in reality they are primarily excuses to spend time with Callahan. The question of maternal guilt over leaving her young children for international trouble zones is given short shrift by a few perfunctory bedtime reading and birthday scenes.

Unnecessarily muddying matters is a vague subplot involving Callahan smuggling weapons and intelligence reports for the CIA -- which he hides in crates of medical supplies -- in return for funding. The narrative, which hedges between a glossy movie of the week on the Lifetime cable channel and a UNICEF travelogue, wanders aimlessly from one hotspot to the next -- making pit stops in Africa and Cambodia -- before going down in flames in an implausible and hokey ending in Chechnya.

While Jolie's passion for the issues explored is clearly evident, her presence, coupled with the film's episodic globetrotting format, makes it play like a sequel to "Tomb Raider" -- "Lara Croft: Red Cross Worker." The movie's humanitarian message never evolves past preachy we-are-the-world moralizing. In the absence of any real dialogue, the characters lecture viewers with heavy-handed homilies that become more tedious with each delivery. What the filmmaker has crafted is not so much drama, or even melodrama, but a big-budget U.N. infomercial slickly packaged with an A-list star -- an Epcot version tour of Third World misery.

Despite its overall superficiality, "Beyond Borders" raises important questions concerning our responsibility to help those in dire need around the world. Its disturbing images -- including a computer-enhanced Ethiopian child ravaged by hunger -- stay with you long after you leave the theater, serving as a haunting reminder that the Christian faith demands more than just passive condemnation of the evil which causes such misery. It demands active participation in alleviating suffering through compassion and self-sacrifice.

While the film's road to the big screen was undoubtedly paved with good intentions, a more apt title may have been "Beyond Boredom."

Due to some war violence, several disturbing images of famine and disease, an implied sexual encounter, recurring rough and crude language and profanity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
